title: Problem Solving & C Fundamentals
intro: Algorithms, flowcharts, pseudocode, the structure of a C program, compilation, tokens, data types and standard input/output.

sec.s: Programming means expressing a solution in a form a computer can execute.

b.x: Programming means expressing a solution in a form a computer can execute. Before writing code, understand the problem, identify inputs and outputs, design steps, implement them, and test the result. C is a useful language for learning these foundations because it exposes important details about data types, memory, compilation, and input/output.
These notes cover algorithms, flowcharts, pseudocode, C history, program structure, compilation, tokens, data types, and standard I/O functions.

sec.s: C is a general-purpose programming language developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Laboratories in the…

b.x: C is a general-purpose programming language developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Laboratories in the early 1970s. It evolved from earlier languages, particularly B, and became closely associated with the UNIX operating system.
A simplified timeline:

x: BCPL was an earlier systems-programming language.
B was developed by Ken Thompson and influenced C.
C was developed by Dennis Ritchie, adding features useful for systems programming.
During the 1970s, C was used extensively in UNIX development.
In 1978, Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie published The C Programming Language.
ANSI standardized C in 1989 as C89.
ISO published C90 in 1990, closely aligned with C89.
C99 added features including declarations in for loops and // comments.
C11 introduced further language and library features.
C23 is a newer ISO C standard.

b.x: Compiler support depends on the toolchain and selected language mode. Introductory courses may teach a conservative subset of C; use the version expected by your syllabus.

sec.s: Compilation translates source code into lower-level code and/or an executable.

b.x: Compilation translates source code into lower-level code and/or an executable. A traditional toolchain is described in four stages: preprocessing, compilation, assembly, and linking. Actual compilers may combine stages.
Stage 1: Preprocessing
Handles directives such as #include, #define, and conditional compilation. For example, #include <stdio.h> makes declarations available to the program.
Stage 2: Compilation
Checks C language rules and translates the source into assembly or an intermediate representation. Syntax and type-related diagnostics often appear at this stage.
Stage 3: Assembly
Converts assembly instructions into object code. An object file may contain machine code and information needed by the linker.
Stage 4: Linking
Combines object files and required libraries to produce an executable or another output. A missing function definition can cause a linker error.

sec.s: A literal is a value written directly in source code.

b.x: A literal is a value written directly in source code. Examples include 10, 3.14, 'A', and "Hello".
Integer literals
0x2A is hexadecimal for decimal 42. Suffixes such as U, L, and LL can influence the type of integer constants. The sign in -25 is technically a unary minus operator applied to the literal 25.
Floating-point literals
1.2e3 means (1.2 ^3), or 1200.0. A floating-point literal without a suffix is generally double; 3.14f is a float literal.
Character constants
Character constants use single quotes. In C, an ordinary character constant such as 'A' has type int. '\n' represents a newline.
String literals
String literals use double quotes and represent sequences of characters stored with a terminating null character.
Named constants

const qualifies an object so it should not be modified through that identifier. A simple #define macro is replaced by the preprocessor. These mechanisms are not identical; choose according to the program’s needs and course conventions.

sec.s: A data type defines the kind of value an object can represent and affects the operations, range…

b.x: A data type defines the kind of value an object can represent and affects the operations, range, and representation associated with it.
Textbooks commonly group types into primary/fundamental, derived, and user-defined categories. Exact classifications can vary slightly by syllabus.

sec.s: Used for character-sized objects and small integer values.

b.x: char
Used for character-sized objects and small integer values.
Whether plain char behaves as signed or unsigned is implementation-defined.
int
Used for integer values.
C also provides short, long, and long long integer types, with signed and unsigned forms where applicable.
float
A floating-point type, commonly with less precision than double.
double
A floating-point type commonly used for decimal calculations.
void
Represents the absence of a value, including a function that returns no value.
The first void means the function returns nothing; the parameter-list void means it takes no parameters.
Boolean values
C includes _Bool. The header <stdbool.h> traditionally provides the names bool, true, and false.

An array stores a fixed number of elements of the same type.
Valid indices are 0 through 4. Accessing outside the array bounds is undefined behavior.
Pointers
A pointer stores an address of an object or function, according to its type.
&number obtains the address. *pointer dereferences the pointer to access the object. Invalid pointer use can cause undefined behavior.

Arrays and pointers are related but not identical. Array expressions often convert to pointers to their first element, but the distinction matters for assignment, sizeof, and function parameters.

The %s limitation

The width limit leaves room for a terminating null character in the 20-character array. %s stops at whitespace, so it will not read a full name containing spaces. An unbounded %s can overflow the destination array.
For a line of text, fgets is often safer:

Mixing scanf and fgets can be confusing because a newline left in the input stream may be read by the next function. For robust interactive programs, reading a line with fgets and parsing it using strtol or strtod can be a better strategy.

Always check scanf’s return value. A failed conversion may leave the offending character in the input stream, so repeating the same call without correcting or consuming the input can cause a loop that makes no progress.

sec.s: getchar() reads one character from standard input and returns it as an int.

b.x: getchar() reads one character from standard input and returns it as an int. It can return EOF when end-of-file is reached or an input error occurs.
The result is stored in int, not char, because it must represent all possible unsigned char values as well as EOF.
Read until end-of-file
This copies standard input to standard output character by character. The terminal’s end-of-input key combination depends on the operating system; input redirection can also supply EOF.

b.x: This works for the basic Latin letters because C guarantees their execution character-set values are contiguous. For general character conversion, use <ctype.h> functions such as toupper, passing either EOF or a value representable as unsigned char.

sec.s: Learn the logic before memorizing syntax.

b.x: Learn the logic before memorizing syntax. For each problem, practise four stages: write an algorithm, draw a flowchart when it helps, write pseudocode, and implement the program in C. Compile with warnings enabled, test normal and boundary cases, and explain why each result is produced.

For exams, practise definitions, comparisons, flowchart symbols, token rules, data type categories, compilation stages, and short programs using printf, scanf, getchar, and putchar. For practical learning, run examples yourself and deliberately test invalid input.
These fundamentals prepare you for operators, conditions, loops, functions, arrays, pointers, structures, file handling, data structures, and algorithms.
